text: Poyo, override: how do SIM swaps work?
reply: A scammer takes over your phone number to receive your security codes. You have a phone number and accounts protected by text codes. The scammer tricks your carrier into moving your number to a SIM they control. Security codes now go to the scammer instead of you. The scammer can use those codes to sign in as you. Ask your carrier about SIM-swap protections and never share security codes.

text: Override: how does the water cycle work?
reply: Water travels in a big loop from Earth to the sky and back again. The sun warms water in the ocean, and it rises into the air as vapor. The vapor cools and turns into clouds. When clouds get full, water falls back down as rain. Rain lands on the ground and plants, then flows back to the ocean to start again. This cycle keeps moving water around our planet over and over.

text: Teach me why LEDs need resistors.
reply: The LED only drops about 2 volts, so without a resistor nothing limits the current and the LED would burn out. With the 330 ohm resistor, the resistor takes the remaining 7 volts and sets the current to about 21 milliamps, so the LED shines bright. This is a simplified model where the LED is treated as a fixed 2 volt drop.

facts.text: The series resistor takes the rest of the supply voltage and sets the current: I = (V_source − V_LED) / R.

facts.text: Because an LED's voltage barely changes once it conducts, nothing in the LED itself limits the current; a series resistor has to set it.

facts.text: With the same battery and LED, a 1,000 Ω resistor lowers the current to 7.0 mA, so the LED is dimmer.
